tagline: From Gettysburg to Monticello, old trade routes meet canals and railways
intro: The Journey Through Hallowed Ground runs from Gettysburg to Monticello, passing through Maryland’s Catoctin Mountain country and Virginia’s rolling Piedmont hills at Culpeper. The 180-mile route received National Scenic Byway designation in 2009. Its organizing partnership presents the road as a way to explore the region’s scenic and historic landscape, with a corridor plan intended to conserve its cultural and natural resources. Maryland’s tourism office describes 57 miles between Emmitsburg and Point of Rocks, with a suggested driving time of two to four hours.

Parts of the byway follow the Old Carolina Road, one name used for several colonial routes. Manufactured goods traveled south along the central Virginia route, while hides, indigo and money went north. Drovers moved cattle, sheep, swine and turkey flocks along it. The modern designation joins US 15 and US 15 Business with Virginia Routes 20, 231, 22 and 53.

Heading south from Gettysburg, US 15 leads through Thurmont toward Frederick. The Maryland stretch includes Catoctin Furnace, where interpretation turns attention to the free and enslaved workers who made iron here. At Point of Rocks it crosses the Potomac toward Leesburg. Continue through the US 15 corridor at Culpeper and Gordonsville before the Virginia roads carry the journey to Monticello.

moments.title: Catoctin Furnace
moments.text: Company-owned stone and log houses once housed Catoctin Furnace’s workers. Four Johnson brothers built the furnace in 1774 to turn locally mined hematite into pig iron. Free and enslaved ironworkers made shells for the Battle of Yorktown. The furnace closed in 1903, and many residents had to find work elsewhere. When the property changed hands in 1923, resident families could buy their houses. Interpretive panels on the African American Cemetery Trail explain ironmaking and the lives of workers buried here. The Museum of the Ironworker displays forensic facial reconstructions of two enslaved ironworkers, alongside clothing and other artifacts.

moments.title: Point of Rocks
moments.text: A narrow gap between the Potomac River and Catoctin Mountain forced two transportation companies into a contest for space. In 1828, the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal and Baltimore and Ohio Railroad went to court over the right-of-way west of Point of Rocks. After six years they agreed to share it. The railroad later tunneled through the mountain in 1867. The town’s Gothic Revival brick station stands at the junction of two rail lines, another expression of the connections concentrated here. E. Francis Baldwin designed the station. Point of Rocks remains a passenger stop on the MARC Brunswick Line.

moments.title: Gordonsville
moments.text: Nathaniel Gordon’s tavern stood at the meeting of two highways, serving stage-route travelers before the railroads reached Gordonsville. In 1854 the Orange & Alexandria Railroad completed its line into town, strengthening its role as a transportation hub. The original tavern burned in 1859; the Exchange Hotel followed in 1860 to serve rail passengers and other travelers. During the Civil War, the hotel became a receiving hospital. The building is now the Civil War Exchange Museum, preserving a different chapter from the tavern’s stagecoach years. Later roads and rail lines bypassed the town, and Gordonsville became a rural market center as the transport connections shifted.
